control_flow.quote: At the if nothing happens yet; Then x becomes 10; so x > 5 is true and the if prints big
control_flow.rule: wrong rule: An if statement watches its condition while the program runs and fires as soon as the condition becomes true (if = whenever). Right rule: An if condition is tested once, when control reaches the if statement; later changes to the variables do not trigger the branch.

evidence.label: shown
evidence.quote: At the if nothing happens yet; Then x becomes 10; so x > 5 is true and the if prints big
evidence.logic: Folk meaning: English 'if' (and 'whenever') states a standing rule that stays in force and fires whenever its condition becomes true. A Java if is evaluated once, when control reaches it, and then is 'taken off the books'; changing the variables later does not re-trigger it.

evidence.label: shown
evidence.quote: At the if nothing happens yet; because x is 1; so x > 5 is true and the if prints big
evidence.logic: Applies the if rule (LT) unevenly: tests the condition on some visits but not others (e.g. runs the branch on every loop pass without testing), runs the branch after a false test, or re-checks the condition after the branch has run. (here mixing in: "an if body repeats while its condition holds")

evidence.label: shown
evidence.quote: At the if nothing happens yet; Then x becomes 10; so x > 5 is true and the if prints big
evidence.logic: Folk meaning: in everyday instructions a listener reads the whole list at once, does steps in a sensible order and infers what the writer wants. Java instead executes statements one at a time, top to bottom, each only when control reaches it, and nothing later in the program has any effect earlier.
